title: The Reptile With a Third Eye
publisher: British Journal of Ophthalmology (BMJ), via PubMed Central
quote: The tuatara has a third eye, as do some other reptiles. ... In the tuatara, as in the other reptiles with the organ, the third eye is a dorsal midline structure just ventral to a parietal plug which is homologous to, and resembles, a cornea. ... The third eye, then, represents evolution's earlier approach to photoreception. ... Why should the photoreceptors be everted in the third eye but not in the lateral eyes? ... If the development of the third eye seems mysterious, the function is even more obscure.
correctedFact: Tuataras have a real third eye on top of the head, with its own lens and a light-sensing retina tucked under a cornea-like plug. Weirder still, its photoreceptors face the opposite way to those in the regular eyes, and what the eye actually does remains a mystery.
note: Third eye hook saved (Schwab and O'Connor 2005). The rest of the card is still as the first pass left it: 'live past 100' (DOC says up to 100), 'predates the dinosaurs' (this paper says the order's heyday was 200 to 100 million years ago) and 'metabolism' are unsupported, so correctedFact is an optional one-point rewrite on the hook alone.

title: Two-Hour Breath Holders
quote: Biologists have recorded them diving up to 2 kilometres deep and holding their breath under water for up to 2 hours. ... Their enormous volume of blood stores oxygen, which they use very efficiently. They even have extra spaces called sinuses in their abdomens to store extra blood. ... These extra red blood cells make elephant seals' blood very thick. Their muscles are also used to store oxygen. Molecules of oxygen-carrying myoglobin are present in the muscles and colour them black.
correctedFact: Southern elephant seals have been recorded diving up to 2 kilometers deep and holding their breath for up to two hours. The trick is oxygen storage: a huge volume of extra-thick blood, spare blood parked in sinuses in the belly, and muscles so loaded with oxygen-carrying myoglobin that they turn black.
note: Two hours is supported for southern elephant seals specifically (2 km, not 'over 2,000 m'); 'longer than almost any other mammal' not on page. The lung collapse and heart-rate mechanism is on the first-pass NPS page, not this one, so it was swapped for this page's blood and myoglobin mechanism. UCSC Science Notes (northern seals, two hours) was down (503).

title: Built-In Measuring Tape
pageTitle: Cats are (almost) liquid! Cats selectively rely on body size awareness when negotiating short openings
quote: Cats are also aided by their large and sensitive vibrissae, which are positioned on such locations of their head that the cat can detect nearby obstacles in closer encounters. ... Therefore, it is possible that cats approached the narrow openings in our experiment without differential hesitation, and they could use their vibrissae to assess the suitability of the apertures before penetrating them. ... Cats hesitated more when they approached the shortest opening than in the case of the tallest ones.
correctedFact: Cats walk right up to narrow gaps without hesitating, and a 2024 study suggests why: their big, sensitive whiskers sit where they can detect nearby obstacles up close, so cats may use them to size up an opening before squeezing in. Low openings are another story, and those made cats slow down and stop.
note: The 'whiskers as wide as the body' rule is not in this or any credible source found; the peer-reviewed study supports whisker gap-checking only as a hedged possibility. 'Measuring tape' implies the width rule, hence the new title.

title: Always Running Warm
careAdvice: often need sweaters in winter; They also need regular baths since their skin oils have nowhere else to go.
note: Searched web and Europe PMC for Sphynx or hairless cat body temperature, metabolic rate and thermoregulation; read Mota-Rojas et al. 2021 (Animals, PMC8697956: hairless animals are more sensitive to extreme temperatures and prone to sunburn, no temperature or metabolism figure) and two cat thermometry papers (PMC11606290, PMC12298758: only 1 to 2 Sphynx, no breed result). Only pet blogs make the claim.

title: Married for Twenty Years
publisher: UC Berkeley PhD dissertation (Roy Caldwell lab), eScholarship, University of California
pageTitle: The Evolution of Social Monogamy and Biparental Care in Stomatopod Crustaceans (Wright 2013)
quote: Lysiosquillina maculata, displays a division of labor in which males forage and provision females (Caldwell 1991). Caldwell (1991) proposed that in large Lysiosquillids, such as L. maculata, the cost of constructing extensive, mucus-lined burrows maintains monogamy. ... if large adults of either sex desert and are unable to find a new mate with a burrow, they are unable to generate enough mucus to build a stable burrow. ... Among the Lysiosquilloidea, all known members of the Lysiosquillidae display long-term social monogamy
correctedFact: Lysiosquillina maculata mantis shrimp are long-term couples. A pair shares one extensive, mucus-lined burrow and splits the chores: the male forages and brings food home to the female. Leaving is risky, because a big adult that deserts and finds no new mate with a burrow cannot make enough mucus to build a stable one.
note: The 20-year pair is not in the dissertation (the only duration given is lab pairs of a different genus, Pullosquilla, stable for at least four years) and appears only on a resort blog. Species, long-term monogamy and the shared burrow are now supported; 'mate for life' and '20 years' are not. The card's 'fearsome punch' is also off: lysiosquillids are spearers.

title: Flying Backwards, Sleeping Like the Dead
publisher: Journal of Experimental Biology (Sapir and Dudley 2012), abstract via Europe PMC
pageTitle: Backward flight in hummingbirds employs unique kinematic adjustments and entails low metabolic cost
quote: Backward flight is a frequently used transient flight behavior among members of the species-rich hummingbird family (Trochilidae) when retreating from flowers, and is known from a variety of other avian and hexapod taxa ... We unexpectedly found that V(O2) in sustained backward flight is similar to that in forward flight at equivalent airspeed, and is about 20% lower than hovering V(O2). For a bird that was measured throughout a range of backward airspeeds up to a speed of 4.5 m s(-1) ...
correctedFact: Hummingbirds often fly backward to retreat from flowers, and it turns out to be cheap. In a wind tunnel, Anna's hummingbirds held steady backward flight that cost about 20% less energy than hovering, and one bird reversed at up to 4.5 meters per second. Other birds can fly backward too, but hummingbirds make a habit of it.
note: 'The only birds that can fly backwards' is contradicted: the paper says backward flight is known from a variety of other bird taxa. Torpor dropped to keep one point; it stays supported by the Smithsonian page and could be its own card.

title: Ocean's Biggest Brain
publisher: Journal of Ethology (Ari and D'Agostino 2016), abstract via Europe PMC
pageTitle: Contingency checking and self-directed behaviors in giant manta rays: Do elasmobranchs have self-awareness?
quote: Manta rays have a high encephalization quotient, similar to those species that have passed the mirror self-recognition test, and possess the largest brain of all fish species. In this study, mirror exposure experiments were conducted on two captive giant manta rays to document their response to their mirror image. The manta rays did not show signs of social interaction with their mirror image. However, frequent unusual and repetitive movements in front of the mirror suggested contingency checking; in addition, unusual self-directed behaviors could be identified when the manta rays were exposed to the mirror. The present study shows evidence for behavioral responses to a mirror that are prerequisite of self-awareness
correctedFact: Manta rays, giant mantas included, have the largest brain of any fish. Faced with a mirror, two captive giant mantas did not treat the reflection as another ray. Instead they made unusual, repetitive movements in front of it and showed odd self-directed behaviors, responses researchers call a prerequisite of self-awareness.
note: Abstract says largest brain of all fish (not 'relative to body size'); the mirror versus blank panel time and bubble blowing are not in the abstract (full text paywalled, ResearchGate and Springer blocked). 'Ocean's biggest' would include whales, hence the new title.

title: Thirty Years in One Anemone
publisher: Journal of Fish Biology (Buston and Garcia 2007), abstract as indexed by OpenAlex
pageTitle: An extraordinary life span estimate for the clown anemonefish Amphiprion percula
quote: Based on this model, it is estimated that the life expectancy of female A. percula, the oldest individuals in the population, is 30 years. This estimate is two times greater than the longevity estimated for any other coral reef damselfish and six times greater than the longevity expected for a fish of that size.
correctedFact: Female clown anemonefish, the oldest fish in their population, have an estimated life expectancy of 30 years. That is twice the longevity estimated for any other coral reef damselfish, and six times what you would expect from a fish that small.
note: 30 years and twice any other damselfish are confirmed (doi 10.1111/j.1095-8649.2007.01445.x; Wiley and Digital.CSIC pages blocked, so the abstract was read from the OpenAlex index). 'Queuing for decades' and 'in one anemone' are not in the abstract; replaced with the six-times-for-its-size detail.

title: Calls Below Human Hearing
publisher: Journal of Experimental Biology (Garstang et al. 1995), abstract via Europe PMC
quote: Meteorological measurements show that strong temperature inversions form at the surface before sunset and decay with sunrise, often accompanied by calm wind conditions during the early evening. ... The results suggest that the range over which elephants communicate more than doubles at night. Optimum conditions occur 1-2 h after sunset on clear, relatively cold, calm nights. At these times, ranges of over 10 km are likely, with the greatest amplification occurring at the lowest frequency tested.
correctedFact: Elephant calls travel farther after dark. On the Namibian savanna, strong temperature inversions form near the ground just before sunset, and the range over which elephants can communicate more than doubles at night. The best conditions arrive 1 to 2 hours after sunset on clear, calm nights, when calls likely reach over 10 kilometers.
note: Dusk inversions and longer range at night saved. The 14 Hz floor, hearing only the harmonics and the calling peak were not found: Cornell ELP pages, the JEB site and PubMed all returned 403 or a captcha; secondary summaries give Payne et al. 1986 as 14 to 24 Hz but it was not read. Title rests on the unread figure, hence the new title.
